claims.statement: Inventory, expiry, consumption and reorder tracking are recognized operational controls for testing sites.
A clinic-to-clinic medicinal-product exchange is not a lawful default; returns described by EMA are to the original supplying wholesaler.
IVD distributors have traceability and storage or transport obligations, making disposition a licensed-partner workflow rather than a startup-controlled action.
The Polish venue base is numerically large enough for a multi-thousand-site outcome, but the qualified subset is not established.
Low-stock alerts, date alerts, lot tracking and reorder reports are already sold by general and clinic-specific incumbents.
Published price anchors make 180-280 PLN per site plausible as a test range, not as demonstrated willingness to pay in Poland.
Instrumented hospital inventory programs can reduce expiry, waste and owned inventory, but transfer to small clinics is uncertain.
No public evidence reviewed establishes access to a Polish wholesaler's portal, order history, lot or expiry feed for this startup.
No public evidence reviewed establishes a Polish independent-clinic expiry-loss baseline, reliable on-hand counts or a verified shared-savings counterfactual.
The narrowed alert and wholesaler-controlled return-eligibility product avoids the directly evidenced medicine-exchange prohibition, subject to product-specific legal review.

contrary_evidence: EMA directly contradicts the original broad exchange concept for medicinal products; the researched version removes clinic-to-clinic exchange and only signals wholesaler-controlled return eligibility.
Sortly and Bodega already sell overlapping clinic inventory controls at transparent prices, and Cardinal Health has a much deeper enterprise platform.
Hospital savings results are not a conservative proxy for independent clinics with fewer SKUs and weaker counting discipline.
The UDI framework improves traceability but is not evidence of usable lot, expiry, consumption or interface rights.
